straits.live counted 158 AIS-visible ships holding in the Strait and Gulf watch box on 3 Nov; Windward sees 17 empty crude tankers waiting off Fujairah (area approximate).

Gulf crude 16.1 mb/d in Oct, down ~1 mb/d
Kpler: crude and condensate through Hormuz, Red Sea and Gulf of Oman averaged about 16.1 mb/d in October vs 17.09 in September (89% of pre-war 18.0).

US 'defensive' strikes on Qeshm (2 Nov)
The US hit an Iranian anti-aircraft site on Qeshm Island after Iranian fire at a US aircraft; Trump called it a 'minor attack' (exact sites not given).
GULF OIL FLOWS · updated 5 Nov 2026

Less oil is moving out of the Gulf than before the war: Kpler counts about 16.1 mb/d of crude and condensate across Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman in October, down about 1 mb/d from September, and Vortexa puts all Gulf oil exports at 17.1 mb/d vs 18.9 in September. Hormuz itself is nearly shut to visible traffic: Windward counted only 3 crossings on 3 Nov after 7 on 2 Nov, so bypass routes via Yanbu and Fujairah carry over 40% of exports. Attacks continued this week: the IRGC claims four tankers were destroyed by mines south of the strait on 4 Nov and two more tankers and a tug caught fire on 5 Nov (unconfirmed). Brent still fell about 9% on 4 Nov to under $95 as Washington signalled no immediate new strikes after the midterms.

Update: The IRGC claims four oil tankers were destroyed by mines in a prohibited passage south of Hormuz on 4 Nov and two more halted, and on 5 Nov that two tankers and a tug caught fire; none confirmed by maritime authorities.
IRGC (Iran's Revolutionary Guards)
“Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval mines.”
Why it matters: Even unverified, mine claims on the southern lane deter the few tankers still crossing (Windward saw only 3 crossings on 3 Nov) and keep war-risk premiums high, limiting any recovery in Hormuz flows.

Why it matters: With the White House blaming the war for its election defeat and Democrats taking Congress in January, markets price a lower chance of renewed large-scale strikes and a higher chance of a Hormuz deal, pulling the war premium out of Brent.
